text:
Allison Grant: Dropping draft SLOs/alerts for Hosted rollout propagation + policy eval. Need feedback on thresholds + paging policy + runbook links before we lock for GA.

Allison Grant: Proposed SLOs (control plane + propagation):
1) Policy evaluation latency (control plane): p99 < 50ms, p999 < 150ms (per request). Target 99.9% monthly.
2) Policy evaluation availability: 99.95% monthly (5xx + timeouts from policy eval service).
3) Propagation staleness (control -> all Hosted regions): 99% < 60s, 99.9% < 180s. SLI = `now - applied_policy_version_timestamp` at router.

Allison Grant: Alerts draft:
- SEV2 page if propagation staleness p99 > 5m for 10m (per region) OR if any region > 10m for 5m.
- SEV3 (ticket) if p99 > 2m for 30m (any region).
- Policy eval latency: page if p99 > 200ms for 10m AND error rate > 1% (trying to avoid paging on CPU noise).

Allison Grant: Runbook link to include in alert annotations: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/hosted-rollout-pause-and-rollback-runbook

Allison Grant: Open questions:
- Are we OK with 60s target for 99% propagation for GA? Routing folks originally asked for <30s.
- Should we page on staleness alone, or only if we see customer impact (e.g. weight mismatch / split not matching) ?
- Do we need separate SLO for “preview endpoint” effective routing? (Console relies on it)

Sean Gallagher: :eyes: thanks. Overall shape looks right. A couple thoughts:
- I’d be careful with paging on p99 staleness per-region because one noisy region will wake us up a lot.
- For GA I’d rather have a crisp “hard” page: any region staleness >10m sustained OR monotonic version check failures spiking.

Sean Gallagher: Re targets: 30s for 99% feels aggressive given cross-region replication + caches. 60s @ 99% seems more realistic as long as we detect when it goes way off.

Aisha Bello: +1 to Sean. Also: if we’re computing staleness from router’s `applied_policy_version_timestamp`, make sure we’re not counting in-flight rollout edits where the policy is “valid” but not yet committed. I’ve been burned by that SLI definition before.

Aisha Bello: Suggest SLI uses “latest committed policy version” from control plane as numerator, and router reports “applied committed version”. Then staleness = delta between those.

Ethan Park: On our side, commit is atomic (policy write -> version increments -> publish event). But agree you don’t want to compare against “draft”.

Ethan Park: For what it’s worth, after the propagation race fix (monotonic version checks + retries), p99 in staging is ~22-35s across regions, p999 spikes when we simulate region packet loss.

Jordan Lee: For eval latency: p99 < 50ms might be optimistic under high QPS during peak. We’ve seen p99 ~70ms with cold caches. But p999 < 150ms seems ok.

Jordan Lee: Could we set SLO to p99 < 75ms, and make 50ms an internal target? Otherwise we’ll be “burning” error budget constantly.

Allison Grant: That’s fair. We can do SLO p99 < 75ms, p999 < 200ms, and alert thresholds higher.

Mina Haddad: From routing perspective, 60s propagation for 99% is acceptable if:
1) sticky routing doesn’t cause “mixed” variant selection mid-session (we’re pinning at request start)
2) we have an operator escape hatch (force 0% candidate) that takes effect quickly

Mina Haddad: Biggest pain is when weights are inconsistent across regions and customers think “Console says 10% but I see 40%”. So can we add an alert on “weight mismatch” metric if we have it?

Logan Wright: We can emit a metric like `router_rollout_policy_applied_version{region,route_hash}` and compare to control plane `published_version{region}` but we can’t do per-route in alerts without cardinality explosion.

Logan Wright: What we can do: per-region aggregate of “version behind published” count (routers reporting applied_version < published_version). That gives a leading indicator without tagging every route.

Aisha Bello: Yes. That’s the right pattern. Alert on “% routers behind” rather than per-route.

Connor O'Brien: For release train, we should be explicit which alerts are paging during GA week. We can start with fewer pages (staleness hard page, eval availability page) and treat latency as ticket unless combined with errors.

Connor O'Brien: Also need to ensure alert annotations link runbook + dashboard. Can we add the dashboard URL once it’s in grafana?

Rafael Mendes: On runbook: the pause/rollback doc covers “force 0% candidate” + verifying propagation, but it doesn’t yet have “what to do if one region is stuck behind”. I can update with a section: invalidate router cache / restart canary-router pods / check event bus lag.

Sean Gallagher: +1. When we page, we want 3 commands and 2 links, not a novel.

Allison Grant: OK, proposing revised SLO/alerts based on feedback:

Allison Grant: SLOs:
- Eval availability: 99.95% monthly
- Eval latency: p99 < 75ms, p999 < 200ms (99.9% monthly)
- Propagation staleness: 99% < 60s, 99.9% < 180s (monthly)

Allison Grant: Paging alerts (SEV2):
A) Propagation hard stall: any region p99 staleness > 10m for 5m
B) Router-behind indicator: >5% routers in a region behind published version for 10m (needs Logan metric)
C) Eval availability: error rate > 2% for 5m OR 5xx+timeouts > 0.5% for 10m

Allison Grant: Non-paging:
- Eval latency p99 > 200ms for 15m => SEV3 ticket (unless coupled with error rate >1%)
- Propagation p99 > 2m for 30m => ticket

Jordan Lee: Works for me. For A) make sure it’s not only p99. If a single router is wedged but customer traffic is mostly hitting others, p99 may hide it. That’s why I like B) routers-behind %.

Logan Wright: I can add B) metric with low cardinality:
`rollout_router_applied_version_lag_seconds{region}` as histogram, plus gauge `routers_behind_published_ratio{region}` computed in aggregator.

Logan Wright: Caveat: “routers behind” requires a periodic report from routers. We already have heartbeat every 30s, so should be easy.

Mina Haddad: +1. Also can we define “staleness” clock source? Router host clock skew will make that lag weird.

Ethan Park: Good catch. For staleness we should compute in control plane using publish_time and router’s “applied_version_at” derived from router monotonic time? We currently use wall-clock timestamp in the event payload.

Aisha Bello: Recommend: include publish_time in payload, router reports back “I have version X” and control plane computes staleness as `now_control_plane - publish_time_of_latest_applied`. Avoid trusting router wall clock.

Allison Grant: Let’s do that. I’ll note in SLI definition: “computed centrally; do not use router wall-clock”.

Connor O'Brien: For GA checklist, we also need to label which alerts are “new” so oncall isn’t surprised. Can we add these behind the same GA flag until launch week?

Sean Gallagher: Put them live in staging now, prod in “observe-only” for 48h (no paging), then enable paging as we roll out GA flag by region.

Rafael Mendes: I’ll add runbook steps + a small “alert playbook” section:
- If propagation stall: pause rollout (force baseline), check event bus lag, check control plane publish queue, check router rollout-applier logs.
- If routers-behind: restart rollout-applier in affected region, verify versions converge.

Allison Grant: Great. I’ll update the SLO doc + alert rules draft accordingly and link the runbook + grafana dashboard once Aisha wires the panels.

Aisha Bello: I’ll take the action to add dashboard panels:
- propagation staleness (p50/p90/p99) per region
- routers-behind ratio per region
- eval latency + error rate overlays

Allison Grant: Cool. I’ll post updated thresholds in this thread tomorrow AM for final :thumbsup: from Sean + Connor before we merge into slo-toolkit PR.
